title: Batching vs Quality – Experiment Log (workload-aware batching defaults)
content:
Context
- Goal: identify any output-quality deltas correlated with batching-tier changes (fast/standard/cost-efficient) and/or new workload-aware scheduling heuristics.
- What counts as a “quality delta” here:
  (1) semantic regression vs baseline on prompt sets (task accuracy / judge win-rate)
  (2) behavioral regressions: truncation, repeated tokens, format violations, function-call JSON breakage
  (3) streaming UX regressions: chunk boundaries, early partials that change user-perceived quality
- Important: batching should not change the mathematical model output in theory, but in practice we see:
  - different decode step timing / KV cache reuse patterns
  - different floating-point accumulation order / kernel selection (esp. with quantization)
  - different truncation paths when max_output_tokens + queue/backpressure interact

Method (lightweight, iterative)
- Primary harness: slo-tier prompt sets (chat, summarization, code) + a smaller “edge-case pack” we maintain (see below).
- Metrics tracked per run:
  - pass@1 / task score where applicable (code unit tests subset; structured output validity)
  - LLM-judge win-rate vs baseline (small sample) for chat/summarization
  - format compliance: JSON validity, tool-call schema compliance
  - truncation rate (% responses hitting max_output_tokens or internal cutoff)
  - repetition/degeneracy flags (simple heuristics)
  - streaming chunk stats: time-to-first-token (TTFT), avg chunk size, #chunks, % empty chunks
- NOTE: We do NOT attempt to attribute all deltas causally. This log is for “we saw something, here’s the reproduction + likely mechanism + next step”.

Edge-case pack (living list)
- EC-01: Long system prompt + short user message (tests prefix caching + prompt packing boundaries)
- EC-02: Multi-turn chat with tool call; tool schema requires strict JSON keys ordering (tests structured output stability)
- EC-03: Summarization with strict max words (“<= 60 words”) (tests truncation + instruction adherence)
- EC-04: Code generation with trailing whitespace sensitivity (tests repetition and early cutoff)
- EC-05: Streaming “assistant continues after partial” scenario (tests chunk boundaries + content drift)


Experiment Log

[2026-01-16] EXP-001 – Baseline sanity: batching tiers off vs on (no quant changes)
- Model family: Redwood-curated instruct (70B class)
- Hardware: H100 hosted
- Compare:
  A) legacy manual batching defaults (control)
  B) tiered defaults: standard tier selected by policy (feature flag in lab)
- Prompt set: SLO-tier prompt set v0.9 (balanced)
- Result:
  - Judge win-rate: within noise (B -0.2pp)
  - JSON validity/tool-call: no change
  - Truncation: no change
  - Noted: slight increase in “first paragraph feels more generic” flagged by reviewer on 3/120 examples; could not reproduce consistently.
- Notes:
  - Likely non-determinism / sampling variance. Keep an eye but no action.

[2026-01-22] EXP-002 – Streaming chunking differences on fast tier
- Model family: chat-instruct (13B class)
- Hardware: L40S dedicated test cluster
- Compare:
  A) standard tier
  B) fast tier (tighter wait budget)
- Prompt set: streaming UX pack (subset of EC-05 + 20 customer-like chat prompts)
- Observed:
  - Content semantics equivalent, but chunk boundaries differ (more, smaller chunks on fast tier).
  - A few cases where early chunk ends mid-sentence more often in fast tier.
  - Human-perceived quality complaint: “feels choppy” in a live UI with naive rendering.
- Hypothesis:
  - fast tier prioritizes latency -> scheduler flushes smaller decode groups -> chunk size distribution shifts.
- Action:
  - Not a model quality regression, but a product/UX foot-gun.
  - Filed note to docs/console messaging: recommend client-side buffering of N tokens / sentence boundary heuristic if customers care.
  - Follow-up: ask runtime if a “min_chunk_tokens” hint exists / feasible.

[2026-02-03] EXP-003 – Truncation spike in cost-efficient tier under long-output tasks
- Model family: instruct (34B class)
- Hardware: A10G hosted (cost-focused)
- Compare:
  A) standard tier
  B) cost-efficient tier (aggressive batching)
- Prompt set: summarization + report generation (long outputs, 512–1200 output tokens typical)
- Observed:
  - Truncation rate increased: 1.8% -> 6.4% (B)
  - Increased “abrupt ending” complaints in human review
  - Accuracy for “<= 60 words” constraint (EC-03) worsened due to abrupt truncation, not verbosity.
- Mechanism (suspected):
  - Under heavy batching + backpressure, our service-level max request wall-time/overload behavior can trigger earlier cutoffs (customer-visible as truncated completion).
  - More requests accumulate; a subset hits a wall-time limit during decode.
- Status:
  - Reproducible at concurrency >= 48 on A10G.
- Next steps:
  - Coordinate with runtime/SRE on whether cutoffs are due to overload mode or a per-request guard.
  - If overload-mode related: document explicitly + consider tier-specific behavior (cost-efficient should degrade by increasing batching, but not by silently truncating unless explicit load-shed response).

[2026-02-10] EXP-004 – Structured output (JSON) compliance: minor regression with mixed prompt lengths
- Model family: code-instruct (7B class)
- Hardware: T4 lab
- Compare:
  A) standard tier
  B) cost-efficient tier
- Prompt set: tool-calling pack (EC-02 variants + 100 synthetic tool calls)
- Observed:
  - JSON validity: 99.1% (A) -> 98.0% (B)
  - Failure mode: missing closing brace or trailing text after JSON.
- Hypothesis:
  - Not purely batching; likely interaction with early-stop / token budget and/or streaming flush.
  - In cost-efficient tier, longer queue wait + larger effective batch -> increased chance to hit decode-step guardrails / early-stop conditions.
- Notes:
  - Failures correlated with prompts with longer system prefix (EC-01 style).
- Actions:
  - Add these cases to edge-case pack permanently.
  - Recommend guardrail: when tool mode is enabled, prefer standard tier by default (policy-level) OR enforce stricter stop sequence handling.

[2026-02-12] EXP-005 – Quantization compatibility sanity with tiered batching
- Model family: instruct (70B class)
- Hardware: H100
- Compare:
  A) FP16 + standard tier
  B) INT8 variant + standard tier
  C) INT8 variant + cost-efficient tier
- Prompt set: mixed (chat + summarization), includes “factual recall” subset
- Observed:
  - A vs B: expected small quality drop on factual subset (~0.8pp in our proxy score)
  - B vs C: additional drop is small but visible in judge (C -0.4pp)
  - No increase in truncation beyond known EXP-003 scenario (this run not overloaded).
- Hypothesis:
  - INT8 kernels may be more sensitive to kernel selection differences triggered by different batch shapes; cost-efficient pushes shapes into a regime that slightly degrades.
- Decision (tentative):
  - For this model family, recommend INT8 + standard tier as default “cost” path; reserve INT8 + cost-efficient only for workloads that are tolerant (offline/non-user-facing) OR when eval pack passes.

[2026-02-19] EXP-006 – “Repetition loop” reports during overload simulation
- Model family: chat (13B)
- Hardware: L4 hosted
- Setup:
  - Artificial overload: ramp concurrency 32 -> 128 over 3 minutes; enable overload mode.
  - Compare: standard vs cost-efficient tier.
- Observed:
  - 6/200 samples in cost-efficient show short repetition near end (e.g., repeating “In summary,” lines).
  - Standard tier shows 1/200 similar artifact.
- Hypothesis:
  - Could be sampling instability under increased latency / request timeout interplay rather than batching per se.
  - Possibility: partial decode being cut + retried? (Need confirmation; should not happen, but worth checking instrumentation.)
- Action:
  - Ask runtime team to confirm no “retry mid-generation” path exists.
  - Add trace requirement: mark any partial-generation abort reason in spans; correlate with repetition.

[2026-03-04] EXP-007 – Fast tier: slight improvement in instruction adherence (surprising)
- Model family: instruct (34B)
- Hardware: H100
- Compare: standard tier vs fast tier
- Prompt set: “format adherence” subset (strict bullets, strict JSON keys)
- Observed:
  - Fast tier marginally better on a small subset (+0.6pp format compliance).
- Hypothesis:
  - Likely noise. Alternate hypothesis: shorter queue wait reduces timeouts / truncation-related formatting breaks.
- Action:
  - Mark as “interesting but untrusted”; do not message externally.

[2026-03-15] EXP-008 – Max_output_tokens boundary behavior with long prompts (prompt packing)
- Model family: instruct (70B)
- Hardware: H100
- Compare: legacy vs standard tier
- Prompt set: EC-01 + synthetic long system prompts (prompt tokens 6k–12k)
- Observed:
  - 2 cases where completion ends earlier than expected; logs show internal “max_total_tokens” enforcement differed.
- Hypothesis:
  - Scheduler/prefill-decode balancing changed the way we account for available KV/cache headroom.
  - Batching itself not the cause; token accounting path likely.
- Action:
  - Provide repro prompts to runtime; request unit test for “max tokens accounting independent of batch shape”.

[2026-04-02] EXP-009 – Customer-like support agent streaming: perceived helpfulness down when chunks too small
- Model family: chat-instruct (13B)
- Hardware: L40S
- Compare: fast tier vs standard tier
- Prompt set: support-agent roleplay (streaming)
- Observed:
  - Judges sometimes rate fast tier lower because early chunks are terse and hedgy; later chunks recover.
  - This appears to be a judge artifact: when judging only first ~80 tokens, fast tier looks worse.
- Takeaway:
  - For streaming workloads, evaluation must consider full completion, not only first tokens.
  - Also: some customer UIs show partial responses immediately; they may “lock in” user perception early.
- Action:
  - Update eval protocol: for streaming, judge on full text; add separate “first-100-tokens helpfulness” metric to monitor UX risk.

[2026-04-18] EXP-010 – Post-guardrail patch retest (cost-efficient truncation)
- Model family: instruct (34B)
- Hardware: A10G
- Compare: cost-efficient tier pre-guardrail vs post-guardrail (runtime change to overload behavior + queue caps)
- Prompt set: same as EXP-003
- Observed:
  - Truncation: 6.4% -> 2.3% at concurrency 48 (still above standard but improved)
  - Quality (judge): stable within noise
- Remaining risk:
  - At concurrency 64+, truncation climbs again.
- Recommendation:
  - For A10G class, cost-efficient tier should probably be opt-in until we have clearer overload behavior (load shed vs truncate) and better customer messaging.


Open Questions / To Investigate
- Does any tier change affect determinism guarantees (seeded sampling) across retries? If yes, document.
- Can we expose a “streaming chunk smoothing” option or guidance (buffering) to mitigate choppiness in fast tier?
- Should tool-calling routes default to standard tier regardless of global tier, unless customer overrides?
- Need clarity on overload behavior semantics: prefer explicit 429/overload response over silent truncation.

Notes to self / Reminders
- When you see a “quality regression”, first check: truncation/timeouts, stop sequence handling, streaming flush differences.
- Always record concurrency + overload mode state; most scary artifacts only show up under load.
- Add any new repro prompts to the edge-case pack and tag with EXP id.
